title: Tier 2: Representational (~2–10 years)

html:
This marks the first major restructuring: the child’s coordinated sensorimotor systems are internalized into stable representations, concrete concepts tied to specific objects, events, or roles that no longer require the child to be actively manipulating the object to "hold the idea." Fischer emphasizes that at this point children can begin to treat things as having properties more independent of their immediate actions, and he uses pretend/social role play as a clean example of representational skill (e.g., enacting a "doctor" role with instruments). By the end of this tier, thought is still concrete (tied to specific objects or events), yet the child can reflect on actions rather than merely perform them.

Level 1: Single Representations ( 18-24 months)

The child can hold a single concrete idea in their mind without the object being present. This is the birth of symbols and language (the "vocabulary explosion"). They can focus on one property or category at a time (e.g., "This is a dog," "That is a toy"). If you try to tell a 2-year-old, "This is a dog, AND it is a toy," they often get confused. It is either a DOG (real) or a TOY (fake). They struggle to coordinate two contradictory representations of the same object simultaneously. They also tend to represent a toy as "Mine." They cannot simultaneously represent it as "Yours" or "Shared." The concept of sharing requires Level 2 (Representational Mappings), where two people’s ownerships are coordinated.

Example 1: Pretend Play (The "Symbolic" Representation)

The child picks up a banana, holds it to their ear, and says "Hello?" The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

The child is representing the banana as a telephone. They are overriding the sensorimotor reality (it looks/tastes like fruit) with a mental representation (it is a phone). They can hold this single symbolic identity in their mind to execute the action.

Example 2: Deferred Imitation (The "Memory" Representation)

A child watches their father shave in the morning. The child does nothing at that moment. Hours later, the child picks up a toy block, rubs it on their face, and makes a buzzing sound.

Previously, the child would have to imitate immediately while watching. Now, the child has formed a mental representation of "shaving." They held this concept in memory for hours and then "played it back" later. The action is now independent of the stimulus. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Example 3: Naming Explosion (The "Label" Representation)

The child points to a Golden Retriever and says "Dog!" Later, they point to a Chihuahua and also say "Dog!"

The child has formed a single, stable category: "dog". They understand that this sound ("dog") represents a specific type of thing in the world, regardless of size or color. This is the leap from "words as triggers" (previous level) to "words as symbols".

Example 4: Agency (The "Agent" Representation)

The child sees a wind-up toy stop moving. Instead of banging it (Sensorimotor), they hand it to an adult and look expectantly at the adult’s hands.

The child represents the adult as an Agent, a being who can make things happen. They have a single concept: "Adults fix things." They are treating the adult as a tool for solving the problem.

Level 2: Representational Mappings ( 3.5-4.5 years)

The child coordinates two distinct Single Representations into a functional relationship. Instead of activating just one independent concept at a time, the child can now hold two concepts in mind simultaneously and compute the specific link between them; one representation stands for, predicts, or constrains the other-e.g., "the idea of the ball being behind the couch" guiding search, or "the remembered rule of a game" shaping what move is allowed. It’s characterized by mental-to-mental linking: using a representation as an input to transform/update another representation (often in simple if-then, analogy, or role-rule form), so behavior can be guided by what’s absent, hypothetical, or socially defined rather than only what’s currently perceived.

This level is characterized by:

Causality (A→BA \rightarrow B): The understanding that one concrete event or object acts upon another (e.g., "The rain caused the puddle").

Comparison: The ability to relate two objects along a single dimension. A younger child knows "Big," while a child at this level understands "Bigger than" (mapping Object A against Object B).

Social Reciprocity: The coordination of complementary social roles. The child understands that their role (e.g., "Hider") is defined by its relationship to another person’s role (e.g., "Seeker").

Example 1: The "Theory of Mind" Breakthrough (False Belief)

The classic "Sally-Anne" test. Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves the marble to a box. You ask the child: "Where will Sally look for her marble?" The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

Previously, the child points to the box (reality). They can only represent one reality-the current one where the marble is in the box. Now, the child points to the basket. They can map the Real State (marble is in the box) against Sally’s Mental State (Sally thinks it is in the basket). They coordinate two distinct representations of the same event.

Example 2: The "Because" Justification (Causal Reasoning)

The child explains their behavior or a physical event.

"I am crying (Representation A) because I scraped my knee (Representation B)."

A younger child might cry and say "Knee!" (single concept). Now, the child constructs the bridge: the scrape is the cause of the tears. This allows for the first true excuses and explanations.

Example 3: Past & Future (Temporal Mapping)

The child says "after dinner, I get cookie." (sentences are now 5-6 words long)

The child is mapping an event that is happening to an event that will happen. They are constructing a timeline in their head. A sensorimotor child might cry for a cookie, but they cannot understand the conditional logic of "First X, then Y."

Example 4: "Who done it?" (Causal Mapping)

When asked who broke a lamp, the child explains that "The cat broke it" despite not witnessing the event.

They see the broken pieces, access their mental representation of the cat’s behavior, and construct a causal link between the two. They are inferring an invisible history.

Example 5: Socio-Dramatic Scripts (Role Reciprocity)

A child might hold a toy stethoscope (Single Representation: "I am Doctor"). Now, they force you to join the simulation (e.g "I am the teacher, so you have to sit down."). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The child isn’t just acting; they are holding a mental script of how two abstract categories relate. If you stand up, they get mad-not because you physically blocked them, but because you broke the logical rule of the relationship they are representing.

Level 3: Representational Systems ( 6-7 years)

The child integrates multiple Representational Mappings into a complex, interacting system. They can now control two or more sources of information (relations) simultaneously. This level is characterized by:

Multivariate Control: The ability to focus on two changing dimensions at once (e.g., Height and Width) rather than being captured by the single most obvious feature.

Reversibility: The understanding that mental operations can be done in reverse to return to the starting point (e.g., knowing that subtraction "undoes" addition, or that pouring water back into the original glass restores the original level).

Integration of Contradictions: The capacity to synthesize opposing traits into a single concept (e.g., a person can be "nice" generally but "strict" about homework), moving beyond the black-and-white splitting of the previous level.

Remember that " 6-7 years" indicated these abilities are coming online (in Fischer’s terms, they represent "optimal" performance), meaning they are usually only reached with high support (scaffolding, prompts, familiar materials, practice).

Example 1: Conservation of Liquid (The Classic Test)

The child understands that the amount of liquid is conserved after you pour water from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass.

Mapping A: Height (The water level went up); Mapping B: Width (The glass got thinner).

A younger child focuses on just one mapping. "It has more water because it is taller." They cannot compensate for the width. Now, the child coordinates both mappings into a system of compensation; they understand that the change in one dimension cancels out the change in the other.

Example 2: Social Complexity (The "Nice & Mean" Integration)

When asked to describe a parent or friend, the child is able to integrate traits that are superficially contradictory.

Previously, the child may say "Mommy is nice," then, if Mommy yells, the child switches: "Mommy is mean." They struggle to understand how she can be both. Now, the child might say "Mommy is nice, but she gets mean if I don’t clean my room." The child constructs a system where a person can possess multiple, distinct attributes simultaneously depending on the context. They understand nuance.

Example 3: Double Classification (The Matrix)

You give the child a pile of shapes: Red Squares, Blue Squares, Red Circles, Blue Circles. You ask them to sort them into a grid (Matrix); the child now sorts by shape and color, processing two symbolic categories simultaneously. The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

Example 4: The Arithmetic System (Reversibility)

The child understands that subtraction is the inverse of addition.

Whereas a younger child can count, these children understand the logical system of numbers.

Example 5: Intersecting Social Roles

The child understands that a person can hold two roles at once.

Previously, if you say, "Grandpa is also my Daddy’s daddy," the child gets confused ("No, he’s not a Daddy, he’s a Grandpa!"). Now, the child understands that one person can be Grandpa (to me) AND Father (to Dad) simultaneously. They can map the single individual into two different slots in the family system. This schematic maps the article’s main ideas (Figure).
